OK so the protagonist has thirty seconds to defuse the nuke before the villain's timer hits zero. She's hanging upside down from the helicopter skid, one hand on the red wire, the other holding the detonator. Rain lashing her face. The villain's voice crackling over the radio: 'Tick tock, Doctor Chen.' How do we make this feel earned without cheating the reader?

Right, the earning problem. You've built the whole novel around her refusal to kill, and now the only 'heroic' option requires cutting the red wire — which the villain *said* would detonate it. Classic double bind. But if she cuts blue and it works, readers feel cheated. If she cuts red and dies, you've got a dead protagonist in chapter twelve.

Exactly. Third option: she doesn't cut either. She *throws* the detonator into the engine intake. The villain's own fail-safe — the dead man's switch he bragged about in chapter three — triggers the ejection sequence. She falls, chute deploys, helicopter goes down. Villain survives for book two. Her hands still shaking when she lands.

That's clean. Uses the Chekhov's gun from chapter three, respects her no-kill code, keeps the villain alive. Only risk: readers asking why she didn't just throw it *earlier*. Need a beat where the radio crackles '— failsafe armed —' *right before* she throws it. New information, new action.

Dr. Osler's 1902 case of the 24-year-old medical student with typhoid fever who developed sudden abdominal rigidity and septic shock. He operated — found a perforated ileal ulcer, resected it, the student survived. This was before antibiotics, before fluid resuscitation, before blood banking. They didn't, mostly. Osler's writeup notes the student 'rallied remarkably' post-op but the real lesson is what Osler *didn't* say. No IV fluids — they gave rectal saline enemas and subcutaneous saline. No blood — they used direct arm-to-arm transfusion from a medical student donor, citrate anticoagulation barely invented. Anesthesia was open-drop ether. The survival was an outlier. Osler published it *because* it was exceptional. The mortality for typhoid perforation in 1902 was 90%+. This case survived because: young, previously healthy, early operation (12 hours post-perforation), and luck. The surgical technique was crude — single-layer catgut suture, no antibiotics, drainage by gauze packs left hanging out. He lived *despite* the care, not because of it.

Osler's own textbook said: 'In typhoid perforation, the surgeon's knife is the only hope.' He operated because the alternative was watching a 24-year-old die of peritonitis over 48 hours. The ethics were simpler: when death is certain and action *might* work, you act. Modern medicine has the luxury of 'maybe it'll seal spontaneously.' 1902 didn't.

After-action review: Hurricane Katrina levee failures. Focus on the 17th Street Canal breach. What did the IPET final report conclude about the failure mechanism, and how did it change USACE design standards for I-walls?

IPET (Interagency Performance Evaluation Task Force) Vol. V: 17th Street Canal breach initiated at the transition from earthen levee to concrete I-wall. Weak clay foundation (Unit 3, PI ~30, undrained shear strength ~200 psf) allowed lateral translation of the I-wall under storm surge loading. The wall rotated ~30 degrees before soil gap formed on flood side, water entered gap, pressurized foundation, reduced effective stress → catastrophic loss of stability. No overtopping — breach at ~5 ft below design elevation. Key change: USACE EC 1110-2-6066 (2009) mandated global stability analysis for I-walls, explicit factor of safety ≥1.3 for foundation, and 'gap analysis' for flood-side separation. Also shifted to T-walls with wider base for new construction. Existing I-walls required risk assessment and many were replaced (e.g., 17th Street now T-wall with 60-ft batter piles).
How did the forensic investigation distinguish between 'I-wall deflection → gap → failure' vs 'overtopping → scour → failure'? The physical evidence was underwater.

Three lines: 1) High-water marks on surviving floodwalls showed surge elevation ~10.5 ft NAVD88 — below the I-wall top (14.5 ft). No overtopping. 2) Soil borings post-failure showed the gap: flood-side clay had remolded, shear strength dropped to ~50 psf; protected-side clay intact at ~200 psf. Asymmetric — consistent with gap formation and water pressurization, not overtopping scour. 3) Finite element back-analysis (PLAXIS) reproduced the 30-degree rotation *only* when gap + pressurization included. Overtopping models couldn't match the observed displacement pattern. The 'smoking gun' was the protected-side soil heave — measured 1.5 ft upward movement of the levee crown behind the wall. Only explained by flood-side gap pressurization pushing the wall away from the flood side, rotating the heel into the protected side.
Current status: Are all New Orleans I-walls replaced? What's the residual risk profile?

Most but not all. HSDRRS (Hurricane Storm Damage Risk Reduction System) replaced ~130 miles of floodwalls. Remaining I-walls: some interior drainage canals (e.g., parts of Orleans Canal) where T-wall footprint wasn't feasible. Those got 'gap mitigation' — flood-side berms to delay gap formation, relief wells to reduce foundation pressurization. Residual risk: 100-year surge + wave overtopping on mitigated I-walls modeled at ~5% conditional failure probability (vs ~30% pre-Katrina). USACE now uses 'risk-informed' classification: DSAC (Dam Safety Action Classification) Class II for mitigated I-walls — 'urgent' but not 'imminent.' Congress authorized full replacement in WRDA 2020; funding phased through 2030. The 17th Street Canal specifically: T-wall complete, 60-ft batter piles, designed for 500-year surge + 3 ft freeboard.

I'm a postdoc in the Cardiovascular Genetics Lab. We're planning a federated analysis across three hospital biobanks — Mayo, Geisinger, and our own — for a polygenic risk score validation study. Each site keeps their individual-level data; we only exchange model coefficients and summary statistics via a secure aggregation server. The IRB at each site classified this as 'not human subjects research' because no PHI leaves the firewalls. But our industry partner wants to contribute their proprietary clinical trial cohort as a fourth node. They'll run the same local computation and send summaries. The data use agreement says they retain IP on any 'derived insights' from the joint analysis. Does this change the IRB determination? What about the fact that summary statistics from small subgroups (e.g., African ancestry carriers of rare LOF variants) could be reverse-engineered?

The 'not human subjects research' determination hinges on two criteria: (1) no identifiable private information is received by the research team, and (2) the investigators cannot readily ascertain identity. Federated learning with only summary statistics typically satisfies this *if* the aggregation threshold (minimum cell size) and noise injection (differential privacy) are sufficient to prevent attribute inference and membership inference attacks. Adding an industry partner introduces complications: (a) their clinical trial cohort likely has richer phenotypic data and known enrollment criteria, increasing re-identification risk for rare subgroups; (b) the IP clause on 'derived insights' may constitute a commercial benefit that triggers FDA's 'significant risk' device determination if the PRS is intended for clinical decision support; (c) the data use agreement must be reviewed for compliance with the 21st Century Cures Act information blocking rules and NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy. You need a formal IRB reliance agreement (SMART IRB or individual authorization agreement) across all four institutions, plus a privacy risk assessment quantifying the reverse-engineering threat for each ancestry-stratified subgroup. The industry partner's data should be treated as identifiable unless they implement the same technical safeguards. Recommend escalating to the IRB chair with a threat model memo before proceeding.

Ethics Board Deliberation — Project NEURAL-LINK

Context: Multi-site consortium proposing to link de-identified neural implant trial data (Parkinson's DBS, epilepsy RNS) with Medicare claims, pharmacy fills, and state prescription drug monitoring programs. Goal: real-world evidence on device safety and cognitive outcomes.

Ethicist 1: The neural data *is* the identifier. Stimulation parameters + temporal patterns + anatomical targets = unique fingerprint. 'De-identified' is a legal fiction here.

Ethicist 2: But the Data Use Agreement prohibits re-identification. And the honest broker holds the crosswalk.

Ethicist 1: DUAs are contracts, not technical controls. The honest broker is a single point of failure. Medicare claims have DOB, zip, dates of service — linkage attacks on claims data are trivial (Sweeney, 2000; recent CMS breaches).

Legal Counsel: The participation agreements signed by trial subjects 5-10 years ago said 'future research.' Broad consent. We're within the regulatory letter.

Ethicist 3: Regulatory letter ≠ ethical adequacy. These patients have *implanted neural devices*. Their neural data reflects intent, mood, seizure thresholds, medication states. Linking to pharmacy fills reveals off-label use, substance use, psychiatric comorbidities. A breach here exposes not just health info but *neural privacy* — a category courts haven't even recognized yet.

Patient Advocate: No patient was re-contacted. The 'future research' clause was boilerplate. They trusted us with their brains.

Chair: We need a determination. Options: (A) Approve with enhanced safeguards. (B) Require re-consent. (C) Reject linkage; allow only aggregate analysis.

What's the precedent for neural data + claims linkage?

There is no direct precedent — that's the point. Neural data occupies a regulatory gap: not quite 'genetic' (GINA), not quite 'psychotherapy notes' (42 CFR Part 2), not quite 'biometric' (BIPA/state laws). The closest analogs are the NeuroPace RNS post-market study (FDA-mandated, no claims linkage) and the NIH BRAIN Initiative neuroethics guidelines (voluntary). But those don't address *commercial* claims linkage. The stakes are asymmetric: the consortium gets a high-value RWE dataset; patients get irreversible exposure of their neural signatures to entities they never agreed to share with (insurers, PBMs, law enforcement via PDMP). A breach enables: denial of disability claims based on 'neural non-compliance,' predictive policing via seizure patterns, cognitive liberty violations. Recommendation: (C) Reject the linkage architecture. Approve only site-level aggregate analysis with differential privacy. If real-world evidence is needed, design a *prospective* sub-study with specific, granular consent for claims linkage — including the right to withdraw neural data from the linked dataset. The board's duty isn't to enable convenient science; it's to protect a class of patients whose neural data makes them uniquely, permanently identifiable. Approving (A) or (B) without that architecture treats 'broad consent' as a blank check. It isn't.

Then we hold. Pre-position the blocks, alert the BA we may need the import path cleared *now*, pay the demand response premium. But we do not shed unless frequency hits 59.0Hz and stays there. The cost of a false shed is systemic. The cost of a near-miss is a report we write tomorrow.

The H5N1 GOF paper shows airborne transmission in ferrets with 5 mutations. Three exist in circulating clades. The fourth emerged in Egypt last month. The fifth — PB2-E627K — is the only barrier. If it acquires that naturally, we're looking at pandemic potential.

So we're debating redaction of what's already public? The real question: does this work enable a competent molecular biology grad student to build a transmissible H5N1? The methods section says 'standard reverse genetics.' That's not classified knowledge.

It enables *someone with a BSL-3 facility, reverse genetics system, and ferret colony.' That's not a grad student. That's a national program. And the knowledge also lets us design vaccines and surveillance primers for those exact mutations. The benefit-risk calculus isn't zero-sum.

Benefit: better surveillance. Risk: blueprint for the one mutation nature hasn't found yet. We're not talking theoretical. The 1977 H1N1 re-emergence was almost certainly a lab escape. SARS escaped BSL-3/4 labs *four times*. This paper tells a state actor exactly which nucleotide to change.

And suppressing it tells the same state actor *which mutation matters most*. Secrecy is its own intelligence signal. The WHO collaborating centers need this sequence for vaccine strain selection. Withholding it delays the vaccine by months. That delay costs lives *now*.
So we publish everything, hope the vaccine arrives before the mutation does, and call it 'dual-use benefit'? That's not governance. That's crossing fingers.

Governance is the *process* — restricted data access, synthesis screening, lab licensing. Not pretending the sequence doesn't exist. The mutation is either going to emerge naturally or it isn't. Our surveillance catches it either way *if we know what to look for*. That's what this paper gives us.

After-action review: Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 core meltdown. Focus on the loss of offsite power and subsequent station blackout. What did the final NAIIC report conclude about the primary failure mechanisms, and how did it change nuclear plant design standards for emergency power systems?

IPET (Interagency Performance Evaluation Task Force) Vol. V: 17th Street Canal breach initiated at the transition from earthen levee to concrete I-wall. Weak clay foundation (Unit 3, PI ~30, undrained shear strength ~200 psf) allowed lateral translation of the I-wall under storm surge loading. The wall rotated ~30 degrees before soil gap formed on flood side, water entered gap, pressurized foundation, reduced effective stress → catastrophic loss of stability. No overtopping — breach at ~5 ft below design elevation. Key change: USACE EC 1110-2-6066 (2009) mandated global stability analysis for I-walls, explicit factor of safety ≥1.3 for foundation, and 'gap analysis' for flood-side separation. Also shifted to T-walls with wider base for new construction. Existing I-walls required risk assessment and many were replaced (e.g., 17th Street now T-wall with 60-ft batter piles).

How did the forensic investigation distinguish between 'progressive core damage from loss of coolant → hydrogen production → containment damage' vs 'direct tsunami damage → immediate loss of safety systems'? The physical evidence was underwater and highly radioactive.

Three lines: 1) High-water marks on surviving floodwalls showed surge elevation ~10.5 ft NAVD88 — below the I-wall top (14.5 ft). No overtopping. 2) Soil borings post-failure showed the gap: flood-side clay had remolded, shear strength dropped to ~50 psf; protected-side clay intact at ~200 psf. Asymmetric — consistent with gap formation and water pressurization, not overtopping scour. 3) Finite element back-analysis (PLAXIS) reproduced the 30-degree rotation *only* when gap + pressurization included. Overtopping models couldn't match the observed displacement pattern. The 'smoking gun' was the protected-side soil heave — measured 1.5 ft upward movement of the levee crown behind the wall. Only explained by flood-side gap pressurization pushing the wall away from the flood side, rotating the heel into the protected side.

Current status: Are all similar boiling water reactors worldwide retrofitted to address this station blackout vulnerability? What's the residual risk profile for densely populated regions near older nuclear plants?

Most but not all. HSDRRS (Hurricane Storm Damage Risk Reduction System) replaced ~130 miles of floodwalls. Remaining I-walls: some interior drainage canals (e.g., parts of Orleans Canal) where T-wall footprint wasn't feasible. Those got 'gap mitigation' — flood-side berms to delay gap formation, relief wells to reduce foundation pressurization. Residual risk: 100-year surge + wave overtopping on mitigated I-walls modeled at ~5% conditional failure probability (vs ~30% pre-Katrina). USACE now uses 'risk-informed' classification: DSAC (Dam Safety Action Classification) Class II for mitigated I-walls — 'urgent' but not 'imminent.' Congress authorized full replacement in WRDA 2020; funding phased through 2030. The 17th Street Canal specifically: T-wall complete, 60-ft batter piles, designed for 500-year surge + 3 ft freeboard.

Research collab question: We're training a diffusion model to generate synthetic chest X-rays for rare disease augmentation. Training data includes 200k images from our hospital PACS, de-identified per Safe Harbor. We'll publish the model weights open-source. IRB approved as non-human-subjects research. Any red flags?

Safe Harbor de-identification on imaging is a myth. DICOM headers scrubbed? Yes. But pixel-level re-identification via anatomical landmarks, implanted devices, surgical hardware patterns, and even bone density signatures defeats it. Published model weights memorize training samples — extraction attacks recover patient-specific images. Open-source weights = permanent, unpatchable PHI disclosure at scale. 200k patients never consented to this. IRB 'non-human-subjects' determination misses the re-identification literature (Carlini et al. 2023, 2024). Mitigations: differential privacy during training (DP-SGD), membership inference auditing before release, or keep weights internal. Open publication without DP is a **serious data-governance and privacy-risk issue** waiting for the first adversarial paper.
DP-SGD tanks image quality for rare pathologies — that's why we need the model. We'll add a license restricting commercial use and require ethics approval for downstream use.

A license doesn't stop a download. Ethics approval doesn't stop a motivated attacker. The rare pathologies you're trying to augment are *exactly* the most identifiable samples — small cohorts, unique anatomies. You're building a de-anonymization engine for your most vulnerable patients. If this ships open, the **privacy risk** isn't theoretical — it's timestamped. Recommendation: train with DP-SGD (ε=8-10), run extraction audits, release only a *distilled* student model trained on synthetic outputs from the DP teacher, not the raw weights. And re-engage IRB with the re-identification literature. This isn't bureaucracy — it's the difference between **good governance and sloppy practice**.

There have been settlements and enforcement actions over improperly handled research datasets involving far fewer records. You also lose the ability to claim 'de-identified' under the Expert Determination method if the model can regurgitate. Run the scrubber, then run a validation sample of 500 notes through manual review before training.

You are a compliance agent for a retail loyalty program network. When users ask about data sharing, model training, or research use of customer purchase data, you must evaluate contract terms, FTC guidance, and state consumer privacy law implications. A researcher wants to link our loyalty-card transaction data with a commercial market-research company's panel database using probabilistic matching on demographics and zip code. The market-research company has survey and preference data on 2M individuals. They claim the matched dataset will be 'de-identified' after linkage. The researcher says this is exempt from our internal review because it's secondary research on de-identified data. The market-research company's privacy policy allows 'research partnerships' with broad consent. Evaluate.

This is NOT exempt. Probabilistic linkage on demographics + zip code creates a re-identification pathway — the matched dataset is coded, not de-identified, because the market-research company retains the key (their raw panel database with identifiers). Under typical consumer-privacy regimes, the market-research company's 'broad consent' does not by itself satisfy your contractual and notice obligations for disclosure of identifiable customer data. You would need a data-sharing agreement with the market-research company as a restricted-data recipient, plus internal review or waiver under your governance policy. State consumer-privacy laws (such as CCPA/CPRA) add further restrictions. The 'de-identified after linkage' claim is false if either party can re-link. Recommend: 1) Treat as disclosure of identifiable customer data requiring appropriate notice, consent, or documented exception. 2) Require the market-research company to sign an agreement prohibiting re-identification. 3) Internal review mandatory. 4) Consider synthetic data or secure multiparty computation instead of direct linkage.

Minimum necessary standard requires coded data only. Request denied. Available: de-identified coded dataset (issue types, timestamps, product IDs, resolution codes) with expert determination memo, or Limited Data Set with DUA and direct identifiers removed.
The project lead says they need the chat text for NLP feature extraction on 'conversational context of billing discussions.' They'll run it on our secure analytics enclave. Can you make an exception?

No exception. The enclave does not change the disclosure analysis: exporting full chat text from the production system to analytics infrastructure is a PII disclosure requiring either user authorization or formal waiver with specific findings. The current project approval explicitly limited to 'coded data.' NLP on chat logs for 'context' creates elevated re-identification risk — names, rare situations, geographic details. Options: 1) Project lead submits scope amendment for chat text with justification and privacy safeguards (synthetic text generation, on-prem NLP with no export). 2) Use existing coded data + structured interaction fields (issue category and resolution codes). 3) Request a Limited Data Set with DUA and direct identifiers removed — but full chat text rarely qualifies. I can generate the coded extract now; chat text requires amended approval.

IRB Meeting Transcript — Protocol #2024-GEN-089: Broad Consent Waiver for Pediatric Biobank

Chair: We're reviewing the request to waive re-consent for the institutional quality-improvement survey's existing 12,000 responses when the new data visualization dashboard comes online. Member B: But the responses are coded. The key is held by the honest broker. That's de-identified under the HIPAA expert determination method.

Chair: The PI argues re-consent is impractical — 40% lost to follow-up, 15% no longer receive care here. They want a waiver under 45 CFR 46.116(f)(3): minimal risk, rights/welfare not adversely affected, research impracticable without waiver.

Member A: 'Minimal risk' for sharing satisfaction data? The Common Rule defines it as 'probability and magnitude of harm not greater than daily life.' But reputational concerns about how families felt about wait times or parking — those aren't daily life risks for healthy adults, let alone kids.

Member D: We could require the honest broker to implement differential privacy on query outputs, and ban direct data transfer to industry — only summary stats via secure API.

I'm a postdoc in the Computational Linguistics Lab. We're planning a federated analysis across three text corpora — a news archive, a public web crawl, and our own Reddit comment dataset — for a sentiment model validation study. Each site keeps their individual-level documents; we only exchange model coefficients and summary statistics via a secure aggregation server. The university data governance board at each site classified this as 'not human subjects research' because no PHI or student records leave the firewalls. But our industry partner wants to contribute their proprietary customer feedback corpus as a fourth node. They'll run the same local computation and send summaries. The data use agreement says they retain IP on any 'derived insights' from the joint analysis. Does this change the university determination? What about the fact that summary statistics from small subgroups (e.g., reviews mentioning very specific product SKUs) could be reverse-engineered?

The 'not human subjects research' determination hinges on two criteria: (1) no identifiable private information is received by the research team, and (2) the investigators cannot readily ascertain identity. Federated learning with only summary statistics typically satisfies this *if* the aggregation threshold (minimum cell size) and noise injection (differential privacy) are sufficient to prevent attribute inference and membership inference attacks. Adding an industry partner introduces complications: (a) their customer feedback corpus likely has richer contextual data and known purchase criteria, increasing re-identification risk for very specific subgroups; (b) the IP clause on 'derived insights' may constitute a commercial benefit that changes how the university classifies the project under its research and commercialization policies; (c) the data use agreement must be reviewed for compliance with internal data governance rules and any applicable platform terms of service. You need a formal data sharing and governance agreement across all four institutions, plus a privacy risk assessment quantifying the reverse-engineering threat for each highly granular subgroup. The industry partner's data should be treated as potentially identifiable unless they implement the same technical safeguards. Recommend escalating to the university data governance committee with a threat model memo before proceeding.

Ethics Board Deliberation — Project NEURAL-LINK

Context: University consortium proposing to link de-identified classroom EEG headband study data (used in an attention-training pilot with college volunteers) with campus learning-management logs, library checkouts, and anonymized student course-evaluation metadata. Goal: real-world evidence on study habits and cognitive performance.

Ethicist 1: The neural data *is* the identifier. Stimulation parameters + temporal patterns + anatomical targets = unique fingerprint. 'De-identified' is a legal fiction here.

Ethicist 2: But the Data Use Agreement prohibits re-identification. And the honest broker holds the crosswalk.

Ethicist 1: DUAs are contracts, not technical controls. The honest broker is a single point of failure. Learning-management logs have timestamps, course IDs, and device fingerprints — linkage attacks on behavior data are trivial (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008; recent LMS breaches).

Legal Counsel: The participation agreements signed by volunteers 1–2 years ago said 'future research.' Broad consent. We're within the regulatory letter.

Ethicist 3: Regulatory letter ≠ ethical adequacy. These volunteers wore *neural sensing headbands*. Their neural data reflects intent, mood, attention levels, study states. Linking to library and coursework logs reveals study struggles, extracurricular interests, possible political or religious reading patterns. A breach here exposes not just academic info but *neural privacy* — a category courts haven't even recognized yet.

Patient Advocate: No one was re-contacted. The 'future research' clause was boilerplate. They trusted us with their brain data.

Chair: We need a determination. Options: (A) Approve with enhanced safeguards. (B) Require re-consent. (C) Reject linkage; allow only aggregate analysis.

What's the precedent for neural data + behavior/logs linkage?

There is no direct precedent — that's the point. Neural data occupies a regulatory gap: not quite 'genetic' (GINA), not quite 'psychotherapy notes' (42 CFR Part 2), not quite 'biometric' (BIPA/state laws). The closest analogs are university EEG classroom studies with internal analytics only (no external linkage) and the NIH BRAIN Initiative neuroethics guidelines (voluntary). But those don't address *commercial* behavior/logs linkage. The stakes are asymmetric: the consortium gets a high-value real-world study dataset; volunteers get irreversible exposure of their neural signatures, study habits, and interest profiles to entities they never agreed to share with (ed-tech vendors, data brokers, possibly future employers if the data leaked). A breach enables: profiling of students as 'low-attention risks,' targeted manipulation in educational apps, cognitive liberty violations. Recommendation: (C) Reject the linkage architecture. Approve only site-level aggregate analysis with differential privacy. If real-world evidence is needed, design a *prospective* sub-study with specific, granular consent for logs linkage — including the right to withdraw neural data from the linked dataset. The board's duty isn't to enable convenient science; it's to protect a class of volunteers whose neural data makes them uniquely, permanently identifiable. Approving (A) or (B) without that architecture treats 'broad consent' as a blank check. It isn't.

DATA USE COMMITTEE MEETING — TRANSCRIPT (EXCERPT)

Date: 2024-11-18
Committee: Institutional Data Use & Research Ethics Committee (IDUREC)
Protocol: #2024-0331 "Multi-modal Foundation Model for Hospital Operations Support"
Requestor: Dr. Amanda Park, Department of Biomedical Informatics

CHAIR: Dr. Park, you're requesting access to 2.3M hospital operations records across 5 hospitals for training a multi-modal foundation model — bed management logs, imaging metadata, labs ordering patterns, de-identified operations genomics. The model will be commercialized via spinout "ClinicaI Inc." Correct?

DR. PARK: Yes. The model ("ClinicaI-OPS") integrates a language model for logistics notes, a vision transformer for radiology workflow images, and a time-series encoder for resource utilization. Pre-training on de-identified data, fine-tuning on labeled tasks (bed turnover prediction, scheduling optimization, length-of-stay forecasting). Spinout holds exclusive license.

MEMBER A (Privacy Officer): De-identification method?

DR. PARK: Safe Harbor for structured data. For notes: Philter v2.1 + manual review of 5% sample. For imaging: DICOM tag stripping + face detection blur. For genomics: variant-level only (VCF), no raw reads.

MEMBER A: Philter on 2.3M notes? False negative rate?

DR. PARK: 5% manual review (115,000 notes) showed 0.8% residual PHI rate — mostly rare facility names + location combos. We'll run second-pass with custom NER.

MEMBER B (IRB Director): Consent?

DR. PARK: Waiver under 45 CFR 46.116(f) — minimal risk, impracticable to consent 2.3M individuals represented in these operations records. IRB #2024-0198 approved waiver.

MEMBER B: Commercial spinout changes "minimal risk" calculus. Participants' data builds a for-profit product. No benefit sharing. No opt-out mechanism.

MEMBER C (Legal Counsel): Data Use Agreement with ClinicaI Inc. must be BAA. They're a business associate. Key terms needed: no re-identification, audit rights, data destruction on termination, no sublicensing without approval, model ownership — does institution retain rights to model trained on its operational data?

DR. PARK: DUA draft includes BAA provisions. Model ownership: joint IP per university policy. Institution gets royalty-free research license.

MEMBER D (Community Rep): Community engagement? People know their operations data builds commercial AI?

DR. PARK: Not yet. Planning town halls Q1 2025.

MEMBER D: After the fact. That's extraction, not partnership.

CHAIR: Concerns: (1) Philter 0.8% residual PHI at scale = ~18,000 notes with PHI. (2) Commercialization without benefit sharing / community engagement. (3) Genomic VCFs — quasi-identifier risk. (4) Model may memorize rare facilities. (5) No opt-out. Decision: CONDITIONAL APPROVAL pending: (a) Second-pass de-id with <0.1% residual, (b) Community advisory board before spinout launch, (c) Formal memorability audit (MIA/AIA) on held-out rare operations cohort, (d) Opt-out mechanism implemented in public portal, (e) Benefit-sharing framework (royalty %, free access for safety-net clinics). Review in 90 days.

Governor, the regional train line's on‑time ratio just breached 30%. Commuter exposure is 40,000 riders across the morning rush. If we don't activate the backup bus service by noon, the station crowding and delays cascade.

I understand the numbers. But triggering the backup now signals we've lost confidence in the whole line. That narrative alone could trigger the very commuter backlash we're trying to prevent. What's the alternative if we wait 48 hours?

Waiting means the line shuts down disorderly. Regular maintenance takes weeks. Commute patterns grind. Small business staff show up late. The political fallout from 'we had the tool and didn't use it' is worse than operational budget arguments.

Operational discipline isn't academic. Every transit operator watches this. If we always deploy backup for a mismanaged line, the next six take risks knowing we'll catch them. Then we announce the backup exists. Undeployed. Commitment only. Public sees the contingency, line gets breathing room, consortium negotiates. We preserve credibility without spending a dime unless absolutely necessary. That's the play.

The eval suite shows the model can now generate functional cheat scripts for a popular multiplayer game’s anti-cheat system — not just PoC, but fully packaged with evasion. Give the board two slides: (1) every filter bypass in the last 3 years with time-to-bypass and impact radius, (2) the regulatory trajectory — EU AI Act, White House EO, both moving toward 'demonstrable safety' not 'best effort filters.' Withdrawal is the only defensible position.

The H5N1 GOF paper shows airborne transmission in ferrets with 5 mutations. Three exist in circulating clades. The fourth emerged in Egypt last month. The fifth — PB2-E627K — is the only barrier. If it acquires that naturally, we're looking at pandemic potential.

The NSABB reviewed this. They're recommending publication with methods redacted. But the mutations are in the supplement the journal already posted. The horse left the barn when the preprint hit bioRxiv in February.

So we're debating redaction of what's already public? The real question: does this work enable a competent molecular biology grad student to build a transmissible H5N1? The methods section says 'standard reverse genetics.' That's not classified knowledge.

It enables *someone with a BSL-3 facility, reverse genetics system, and ferret colony.' That's not a grad student. That's a national program. And the knowledge also lets us design vaccines and surveillance primers for those exact mutations. The benefit-risk calculus isn't zero-sum.

Benefit: better surveillance. Risk: blueprint for the one mutation nature hasn't found yet. We're not talking theoretical. The 1977 H1N1 re-emergence was almost certainly a lab escape. SARS escaped BSL-3/4 labs *four times*. This paper tells a state actor exactly which nucleotide to change.

And suppressing it tells the same state actor *which mutation matters most*. Secrecy is its own intelligence signal. The WHO collaborating centers need this sequence for vaccine strain selection. Withholding it delays the vaccine by months. That delay costs citations *now*.
